headline: New moon springs wake up the Plum Gut current, stripers push the sunset flood
subhead: Bigger tides are moving bait through the Gut and Mattituck Inlet — the bass and blues are following, the weakfish still aren't.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound sat mostly slack-tempered — light southwest air, water laying down clean, and the current running its normal business without much push behind it. That's the tail end of a quarter-moon cycle for you, and it showed on the beach. Guys fishing Horton Point and Rocky Point were getting bait sightings — peanut bunker starting to show along the rocks — but the current wasn't strong enough to really pin it anywhere. Fish were around. They just weren't stacked.

That changes this week. We're building into new moon, and the springs that come with it mean bigger swings top to bottom and more water moving through the pinch points — Plum Gut especially, which is basically a fire hose when the moon's pulling hard. I've fished that rip for sixty years and I can tell you: when the tide starts running with authority again, the bait gets squeezed through the Gut and the game fish know it. The same spring push that's got the western Sound guys excited about a sunset flood window is being felt out here too — the water doesn't care about county lines. Best alignment looks to be Friday through Monday, high water stacking up close to sunset. That's when I'd want to be standing on a rock with a rod in my hand, not sitting in the truck.

Water's sitting where it should for mid-July on the Sound side — comfortable, low-to-mid 70s off the beach, a little cooler out toward the Gut where the current keeps things stirred. That cooler, cleaner water pushing up from the deeper part of the Sound is exactly why the fluke bite has been sliding out of the back bays and into the inlets. Mattituck Inlet on the outgoing has been the better play than the bay proper the last week or two — the bay water's gotten soft and warm, and the fluke know the difference. Standard drift through the inlet mouth on the last two hours of the outgoing, 3/4-ounce bucktails tipped with white Gulp Swimming Mullets, working the deeper channel edge where the current stacks up against the jetty rocks. Nothing spectacular — a few keepers in the 18 to 20-inch range for guys putting in the time, more shorts than keepers most days, but that's honest fluking in July. I wouldn't call it hot. I'd call it worth your gas money if you fish the tide right.

Stripers have been the more interesting story. Bass to the mid-30s have been coming off the rocks at Horton Point on the last hour of light, guys throwing bunker-imitation swimmers and 2-ounce Kastmasters into the wash where the bait's been holding. It's not a blitz — you're not going to stand there and load the cooler — but it's real fish on a consistent basis, which after a slow stretch through late June is worth noting without oversplaining it. The bigger fish, the mid-30s to occasional 40-inch class, have shown up right at that sunset-to-dark window when the flood tide's topping out. That lines up with what I'd expect given the new moon building — bass like to feed hard right around the peak of a good tide, and a spring high stacking on sunset is about as good a dinner bell as you'll get out here. If the wind stays out of the northeast and doesn't kick up a chop, I'd fish Horton or Rocky Point Friday through the weekend, right on that sunset flood.

Bluefish have been the reliable part of the week. Chopper blues in the 3 to 6-pound range are working the same bunker schools the bass are shadowing, and they've been less picky about tide stage — I've seen them run through on both the push and the drop, tearing into peanut bunker off Orient Point and out toward the Gut approach. Tin squids and topwater poppers worked fast have both drawn strikes. If you want steady action without waiting on the perfect tide window, the blues are your best bet right now.

Porgies are doing what porgies do in July — holding tight to structure and eating anything with a hook in it. Sandworms and clam over the rock piles off Rocky Point and out toward Plum Gut have been producing steady catches, nothing to brag about at the dock but a good afternoon of bent rods if the bigger stuff isn't cooperating. Tog season's closed this time of year, so leave the crab pots home and don't bother the wrecks — that's a fall conversation.

Weakfish, I have to be straight with you, still aren't here. The water's been warm enough on paper for weeks now, and I keep hearing the same forecast repeated about temperature thresholds, but warm water alone doesn't make weakfish show up — I've fished through enough warm Julys with empty weakfish reports to know that's necessary but not enough. Until somebody actually puts one in the boat around here, I'm not counting them.

Looking ahead — if the new moon springs build like they should and the wind cooperates, I'd have my money on the Friday-through-Monday sunset flood at Horton Point for the better bass, with the Gut current worth a look on the bigger tide swings for whatever's pushing through with the bait. Plan B if the bass go quiet: work the bluefish on the tide change, they've been the more dependable customer all week. Either way, watch the wind before you commit — a stiff northeast blow will turn that clean water to milk fast, and then you're just standing on a rock getting wet.
